hero.heading: Learn How to Practice. Then Hear the Difference.
hero.problem: “But I could play it at home!” If that is you, I believe you. Nobody ever showed you how to practice. They just told you to do more of it.
hero.solution: I'm Simon, a music teacher. The Practice Code is everything I teach about practicing, whatever you play: get it right first, aim at a target instead of the clock, and practice what you will perform.

first-steps.heading: Start Practicing the Right Way From the Very First Week
first-steps.lead: Am I talented enough? How long should I practice? Why does it go wrong in the lesson? First Steps answers the questions every beginner asks, and gives parents something better to say than “go and do your practice”.

stakes.heading: Beginners Are Told to Practice. Nobody Tells Them How.
stakes.text: I did my 30 minutes a day as a boy: sit at the piano, play through my pieces, watch the clock. It works, slowly. There is a much better way to start.
items: Playing the whole piece through, mistakes and all
Watching the clock until the 20 minutes are up
"Go and do your practice" becoming a daily argument
Parents who want to help but don't play themselves

items.title: Get It Right First

book.description: The Practice Code by Simon Horsey: seven elements that turn practice into progress on any musical instrument, at any level.
book.audience: For students ready for the full method
book.heading: The Practice Code: Everything Nobody Told You About How to Practice
book.lead: Your lesson isn't where you learn the most each week. Your practice is: about 100 minutes of it, against 30 with your teacher. This book is about making those minutes count, whatever you play.

stakes.heading: “But I Could Play It at Home!”
stakes.text: I believe you. It happens because your brain learns whatever you repeat, wrong notes included. More hours won't fix that. Better practice will.
items: Playing the piece through from the top, again and again
Watching the clock until the 30 minutes are up
Getting it right five times out of ten and calling it learned
Learning it on Tuesday and losing it by Friday
Saving the dynamics for “later”

offer.heading: Seven Elements. No Jargon.

items.title: 100% Accuracy
items.text: Give your brain the right pattern every time. Get it right five times out of ten and you might as well have been watching TV.

items.title: Targets, Not Time
items.text: Ready, aim, fire. Tell your brain where you want to go and stop when you get there, whether that takes ten minutes or forty.

items.title: Small Steps Slowly
items.text: Divide your work into small sections. Twice. Then start with the bars you can't play, not the ones you can.

items.title: Listen
items.text: Put an empty chair across the room and imagine sitting in it. What does your playing sound like from there?

items.title: Set the Scene
items.text: Pencil, metronome, water, phone somewhere else. Sort it out first, so “I'll just fetch a pencil” doesn't eat the session.

items.title: Review, Review, Review
items.text: Music's three Rs. One slow play-through at the start and end of each session keeps this week's work for next month.

items.title: Practice What You'll Perform
items.text: Notes without light and shade aren't finished. Dynamics and phrasing go in from the start, not the week before the concert.

includes: The Accuracy Health Check: one week that shows why pieces fall apart in lessons
Goal-setting sheets, with Jane's worked example
A practice-by-event planner, so practice fits around your real week
Lesson notes and weekly targets to fill in with your teacher
Practice games, including the dice game and practice chess

steps.title: Take the Accuracy Health Check
steps.text: Keep a tally for one week. It surprises most people, and it is where the cure starts.

steps.title: Add One Element at a Time
steps.text: Don't be the hare. One or two new habits a month and your practice is transformed within a few months.

steps.title: Hear the Difference
steps.text: Pieces hold together in your lesson and on stage, because that is how you practiced them.

faqs.a: Yes, yes, YES. Talent is not the issue. Tenacity, not talent, is what gets people there, and this book shows you what to be tenacious about.
Any instrument, any style. It is about how you practice, not what you play.

faqs.q: What level do I need to be?
faqs.a: Any. Beginners build good habits from the start, and advanced players use the same seven elements on harder music.

faqs.q: Should I start with First Steps instead?
faqs.a: If you or your child are in the first year or two of playing, First Steps is the gentler way in. The Practice Code covers the same ground and goes much further.

faqs.q: Is this a new edition of Practice Makes Perfect?
faqs.a: Yes. Same teacher, same ideas, reorganised around seven elements and brought up to date.

faqs.q: I'm a parent, not a musician. Will it help?
faqs.a: Yes. There is a section just for you, starting with what to say instead of “go and do your practice”.

book.closing: Stop Watching the Clock. Start Hitting Targets.

academy.heading: Watch It Done. Then Do It Yourself.
academy.lead: Reading about practice is one thing. Seeing it done at the instrument is another. In the Academy I teach every element on video, then take on the things students ask me about most.

stakes.heading: Knowing What to Do Isn't the Same as Doing It
stakes.text: We have all left a talk full of good intentions, changed for a fortnight and slid back into old habits. I watched it happen after my own practice presentations. The Academy is my answer.
items: Reading about a technique but never quite applying it
Not being sure you are doing it right
Getting stuck on memorizing, sight-reading or nerves
Having nobody to ask between lessons
